title: Cellular respiration
blurb: Trace glucose through glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain, with the location, inputs and outputs of each stage, and explain fermentation.
question: During a 400-meter sprint a runner's leg muscles run short of oxygen and start to burn. Which stage of respiration keeps making ATP, where in the cell does it run, how much ATP does it give, and what builds up in the muscle?

teach.body: Formal definition: aerobic cellular respiration is the catabolic pathway that breaks down glucose with oxygen to make ATP: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ to 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + energy (ATP and heat). Plain English: cells "burn" glucose slowly, in small enzyme-controlled steps, and bank the energy as ATP instead of losing it all as heat. Plants respire too, all day and night. Respiration is not breathing: breathing delivers the O₂ and removes the CO₂.

steps.sub: Cytoplasm: glucose to 2 pyruvate; net 2 ATP; no O₂ needed

teach.caption: Fats and proteins can also enter the pathway (as acetyl-CoA or Krebs intermediates).
Glycolysis runs in the cytoplasm. Note the mitochondria, where the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain make most of the ATP.

teach.caption: The Krebs cycle uses no O₂ directly, but it stalls without O₂ because the chain stops recycling its carriers.

teach.h: The electron transport chain and oxygen
teach.body: NADH and FADH2 carry high-energy electrons from glycolysis and the Krebs cycle to the chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane. As electrons pass along it, the chain pumps H+ ions, and ATP synthase uses that flow to make most of the cell's ATP (chemiosmosis). Oxygen is the final electron acceptor: it takes the electrons and H+ and forms water. The CO₂ you exhale does not come from that oxygen; it comes from glucose carbon released in pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle.

teach.caption: Older textbooks give 36–38 ATP per glucose. The figure differs between texts, so learn the pattern: aerobic far exceeds fermentation.

teach.body: With no O₂, the chain stops, NADH piles up and the cell runs short of NAD+. Fermentation solves this: pyruvate is converted to another product, regenerating NAD+ so glycolysis can keep running. The cell gets only glycolysis's net 2 ATP per glucose. Human muscle makes lactic acid during intense exercise; yeast makes ethanol and CO₂, which is why bread dough rises.

Marcus, a pre-nursing student, sprints 400 meters. At first his muscle cells run full aerobic respiration: glycolysis in the cytoplasm, then pyruvate oxidation, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain in the mitochondria, with oxygen accepting electrons to form water. As oxygen runs short, the chain stalls. Glycolysis keeps going in the cytoplasm for a net 2 ATP per glucose, and pyruvate is turned into lactic acid to regenerate NAD+. When he rests and breathes hard, aerobic respiration resumes.

teach.text: Exam traps: glycolysis is in the CYTOPLASM and needs NO oxygen; the MOST ATP comes from the electron transport chain, not glycolysis or the Krebs cycle; O₂ becomes WATER, while CO₂ comes from pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle; respiration USES O₂ and RELEASES CO₂; lactic acid in muscle, ethanol in yeast; plants respire too.

items: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ to 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + ATP: a catabolic pathway.
Glycolysis (cytoplasm): 2 pyruvate, net 2 ATP, 2 NADH, no O₂.
Pyruvate oxidation and Krebs (matrix): CO₂ released; NADH and FADH2 loaded.
Electron transport chain (inner membrane): most ATP; O₂ is the final electron acceptor, forming water.
No O₂: fermentation regenerates NAD+; 2 ATP. Muscle: lactic acid. Yeast: ethanol + CO₂.

summary: You can now put the stages of aerobic respiration in order with the location, oxygen need and products of each, and explain why the electron transport chain makes most of the ATP. You can also explain oxygen's role, where the exhaled CO₂ comes from, and what fermentation yields in muscle and in yeast.

A.q: Which stage of aerobic cellular respiration produces the most ATP?
A.why: The electron transport chain on the inner mitochondrial membrane produces most of the ATP from each glucose.

whyNot.0: Glycolysis yields a net of just 2 ATP per glucose.
whyNot.1: The Krebs cycle mainly releases CO₂ and loads NADH and FADH2; it makes little ATP directly.
whyNot.3: Fermentation is anaerobic and yields only the 2 ATP from glycolysis.

A.q: Where in a eukaryotic cell does glycolysis take place?
A.why: Glycolysis splits glucose into 2 pyruvate in the cytoplasm, outside the mitochondria.

whyNot.1: The matrix is where pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle happen.
whyNot.2: The inner membrane (cristae) holds the electron transport chain.
whyNot.3: The outer membrane encloses the mitochondrion; no respiration stage runs there.

A.q: What is the final electron acceptor at the end of the electron transport chain?
A.why: Oxygen accepts the electrons at the end of the chain and combines with hydrogen ions to form water.

whyNot.0: CO₂ is a waste product released earlier, in pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle; it accepts no electrons.
whyNot.1: Glucose is the starting fuel, broken down in glycolysis.
whyNot.2: NAD+ picks up electrons earlier (in glycolysis and Krebs) and delivers them TO the chain.

B.q: Which pair of products results from alcoholic fermentation in yeast?
B.why: Yeast fermentation turns pyruvate into ethanol and CO₂; the CO₂ makes bread rise.

whyNot.0: Lactic acid is the product of fermentation in human muscle, not yeast.
whyNot.2: Fermentation happens without oxygen and does not release it.
whyNot.3: Lactic acid fermentation does not produce CO₂, and yeast makes ethanol, not lactic acid.

B.q: The CO₂ a person exhales is released during which stages of cellular respiration?
options: Pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle
The chain on the inner membrane
Glycolysis and the electron transport chain
B.why: Carbon from glucose leaves as CO₂ when pyruvate is oxidized to acetyl-CoA and during the Krebs cycle, both in the matrix.

whyNot.0: Glycolysis releases no CO₂, and lactic acid fermentation in human cells releases none either.
whyNot.2: The chain uses O₂ to make water; it releases no CO₂.
whyNot.3: Neither glycolysis nor the chain releases CO₂.

B.q: In which part of the mitochondrion does the Krebs cycle take place?
B.why: The Krebs (citric acid) cycle runs in the matrix, the fluid inside the inner membrane.

whyNot.0: The inner membrane holds the electron transport chain.
whyNot.1: The outer membrane encloses the organelle; no stage of respiration runs there.
whyNot.3: The cytoplasm is outside the mitochondrion and is the site of glycolysis.

C.q: Which statement about cellular respiration in a green plant is accurate?
options: Plants rely on photosynthesis instead of respiration.
Plant cells respire in chloroplasts while it is light.
Plant cells respire in mitochondria day and night.
Plants respire by fermentation when it is dark.
C.why: Plant cells have mitochondria and carry out aerobic respiration all the time, in light and in darkness.

whyNot.0: Plants photosynthesize AND respire; the glucose they make is broken down for ATP.
whyNot.1: Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis; respiration happens in mitochondria.
whyNot.3: Darkness stops photosynthesis, not aerobic respiration; plant cells keep using O₂.

C.q: During an all-out sprint, Marcus's leg muscle cells run short of oxygen. Which change takes place in those cells?
options: Pyruvate is converted to ethanol and CO₂.
The Krebs cycle speeds up to make more ATP.
The chain keeps running using CO₂ instead.
Pyruvate is converted to lactic acid.
C.why: Without enough oxygen, human muscle relies on glycolysis plus lactic acid fermentation, which regenerates NAD+ and yields 2 ATP per glucose.

whyNot.0: Ethanol and CO₂ are produced by yeast (alcoholic fermentation), not human muscle.
whyNot.1: The Krebs cycle depends on the oxygen-using chain; it slows when oxygen runs short.
whyNot.2: CO₂ cannot accept electrons; oxygen is the final acceptor of the chain.

C.q: A cell completely oxidizes 2 molecules of glucose by aerobic respiration. How many molecules of O₂ are used and CO₂ released?
C.why: One glucose + 6 O₂ gives 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O, so 2 glucose use 2 × 6 = 12 O₂ and release 2 × 6 = 12 CO₂.

whyNot.0: These are the amounts for ONE glucose; the question uses two.
whyNot.2: This is reversed: respiration uses O₂ and releases CO₂ (photosynthesis does the opposite).
whyNot.3: The equation uses 6 O₂ per glucose, so 2 glucose need 12 O₂, not 2.

reteach.title: Cashing a paycheck
reteach.question: Think of glucose as a big paycheck that has to be broken into small bills before you can spend it. How does the cell cash it?

blocks.body: Glucose is a large check: too big to spend directly. Glycolysis is the corner store that cashes a little of it right away (2 ATP), even with no bank open (no oxygen). The Krebs cycle is the teller who processes the rest and fills envelopes (NADH, FADH2), shredding the old check stubs as CO₂. The electron transport chain is the vault that turns those envelopes into most of your cash (ATP), and it opens only when oxygen is there to take the leftover electrons.

steps.label: Corner store
steps.sub: Glycolysis: net 2 ATP, no O₂ needed

steps.label: Teller
steps.sub: Krebs cycle: fills NADH and FADH2; CO₂ out

steps.label: Vault
steps.sub: Electron transport chain: most ATP; needs O₂

blocks.text: No oxygen means the vault stays shut: only the corner store pays out, 2 ATP per glucose (fermentation).

explain.body: ATP stores energy in its phosphate bonds; hydrolyzing the last one (ATP to ADP + Pi) releases it. Respiration: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6 O₂ to 6 CO₂ + 6 H₂O + energy, recharging ADP into ATP.

test.q: Which substances are the reactants of aerobic cellular respiration?
test.why: Respiration takes in glucose and O₂ and releases CO₂, water and energy.

whyNot.0: CO₂ and water are the PRODUCTS of respiration (and the reactants of photosynthesis).
whyNot.2: CO₂ is released by respiration, not used.
whyNot.3: Water is a product of respiration, formed when O₂ accepts electrons.

explain.body: Glycolysis (cytoplasm): glucose to 2 pyruvate, net 2 ATP. Pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle (matrix): CO₂ released, NADH and FADH2 loaded. Electron transport chain (inner membrane): most ATP.

test.q: Which stage releases CO₂ in the mitochondrial matrix and loads NADH and FADH2?
test.why: The Krebs cycle runs in the matrix, releases CO₂ and fills the carriers NADH and FADH2.

whyNot.0: Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm and produces pyruvate, not FADH2 or CO₂.
whyNot.1: The chain uses NADH and FADH2 to make ATP; it does not release CO₂.
whyNot.3: Lactic acid fermentation happens in the cytoplasm and releases no CO₂.

explain.body: NADH and FADH2 hand electrons to the chain on the inner membrane. The chain drives ATP synthase, which makes most of the ATP. Oxygen accepts the electrons at the end and forms water.

test.q: What happens to the electrons delivered to the electron transport chain by NADH?
options: They pass to oxygen, which forms water.
They combine with carbon to make CO₂.
They are used to split water into O₂.
They return to glucose to rebuild it.
test.why: Electrons move along the chain, powering ATP synthesis, and end on oxygen, which forms water.

whyNot.1: CO₂ is released in pyruvate oxidation and the Krebs cycle, not formed from these electrons.
whyNot.2: Splitting water to release O₂ happens in photosynthesis, the reverse.
whyNot.3: Glucose is broken down, not rebuilt, in respiration.

explain.body: No O₂ means no electron transport chain. Cells run glycolysis alone (net 2 ATP) and use fermentation to regenerate NAD+: lactic acid in human muscle, ethanol and CO₂ in yeast.

test.q: How much ATP does a cell gain per glucose when oxygen is absent and it relies on fermentation?
test.why: Fermentation relies on glycolysis alone, which gives a net of 2 ATP per glucose.

whyNot.0: Glycolysis makes 4 ATP but spends 2, so the NET gain is 2.
whyNot.1: 6 ATP overstates glycolysis; the net yield is 2.
whyNot.2: About 30 ATP comes from full aerobic respiration, which needs oxygen.
